frames.narration: Sku-88 has 50 units on hand in Leeds, 6 of them held by other shoppers, so 44 are available. A shopper starts checkout for 2 units. The request carries a unique id, q-501, so a retry would be recognised.

The check and the hold are one conditional update: hold 2 if available is at least 2. Exactly one of two competing requests can win. Here it succeeds, so held becomes 8 and available falls from 44 to 42.
The reservation is stored with an expiry of ten minutes, 14:10, and the shopper is told the units are theirs until then. A timer is set so the hold is released if nobody pays.

At 14:04 the shopper pays. The reservation service checks that the hold has not expired, then turns it into a pick movement of -2 in the ledger. The hold is released as the pick is recorded: on hand drops to 48 and held to 6, so available stays at 42.

The ledger write also wrote an event to an outbox in the same transaction, and a relay publishes it. The warehouse gets the pick instruction. If the event were delivered twice, the second copy would be ignored because q-501 has been applied.

The channel sync updates the website, the app, the stores and the marketplaces. It lags by a second or two, and a marketplace is shown a safety buffer, so the number is a hint. The real check always happens at reservation.
That night the Leeds team counts sku-88 and finds 45 on the shelf, while the ledger says 48. The reconciliation service compares the count with the balance as of the moment of counting.

The correction is a movement with a reason, not an overwrite, so the history shows exactly when and why 48 became 45. The new available figure, 39, goes out to every channel, and no future shopper is promised a unit that is not on the shelf.
